doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: A-A-B form, prediction and surprise in solos
summary: Galper explains how a solo repeats an idea then breaks the pattern, tying it to blues form, the predictive brain and surprise.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: The opinions, at least they’re considered opinions. Because a lot of this stuff isn’t necessary factual yet because all the science has been on the Western part of the music. Note choice. How does the brain pick a particular note? It’s totally bogus. It’s the rhythm that picks the notes. That’s the African part. And there’s hardly any neurological studies on the African part of the music. None. The rhythm, the beat. What is that? How does a beat go through the air and make people tap their feet? You know. What is it? What’s the quality? I think I figured it out. I think I figured out what groove is, but I’m not a scientist enough to be able to prove it, and I’ve done so much research on this fucking book — sorry — on this book, that I’m researched out and I really can’t do any more on it, I’ve got to leave it up to other people who might be interested in following it up. But I’ve discovered some — like A-A-B, the A-A-B format, all right? You listen to a lot of jazz solos you hear [scats] A [scats] B. Why? Why B? When you play A you hit the expecting part of the brain expects A again, and you play A again. That sets a pattern. The predictive part of the brain then is expecting A a third time but you don’t play A a third time, you use A2 as a bridge the third time into A3 and your solo takes off. It’s magical. I’ve been doing it all my life and I didn’t realize it until I discovered this like early last year. A-A-B. Idea-Idea creates a problem. When you interrupt the two A’s and you don’t do A3, you have a problem that needs to be solved and you improvise the solution.
While you’re describing that it reminds me of blues lyrics.

That form is throughout the music. Listen to Bird. Listen to swing players. I’m not even sure — I’ll tell you this I wasn’t aware I was doing it but I’ve been doing it all my career because I’ve been copying guys who did that, without knowing why. It’s amazing. It has to do with the predictive parts of the brain, the thing that keeps one interested in the music is surprise. It has to be surprised. You have to be surprised as a player. All right?
You don’t want to be predictive. It’s to surprise you, otherwise it’s not going to surprise the audience.
And who was it that said jazz is the sound of surprise?
